ut_logan_canyon.blurb: Logan Canyon is a limestone sport-climbing canyon in the Wasatch Range, a short drive from the town of Logan in Cache Valley, northern Utah, with some quartzite crags as well. Sport routes dominate by a wide margin, with bouldering, trad and top-rope making up the rest. Grades peak from 5.10 to 5.13, with 5.11 the sweet spot, plus a decent supply of easier warm-ups and a few at 5.14. More than thirty crags are scattered up the canyon, and China Wall, Fucoidal Quartzite and Mile 385 are among the busiest. Winter is cold and rock climbing is largely off the table, but most crags catch sun, so chilly days can still be pleasant. Fall and spring are especially appealing.

wi_northwest.blurb: Northwest Wisconsin spans the Lake Superior lowlands, the Penokee Range and the St. Croix River country. Bouldering is the largest part, followed by sport, trad and top-rope. Interstate Park on the St. Croix holds the biggest cluster, with roped climbing and bouldering on billion-year-old basalt that is highly textured in places and smooth in others. Willow River State Park is mostly steep sport climbing above a river, with most routes between 5.11 and 5.13, while Old Grade Road, Apostle Islands and Blue Hills add smaller pockets. Boulder problems are mostly easy to moderate, about VB to V5, and roped climbs mostly run from 5.8 to 5.12 with a few harder.

ca_lost_sierra_the.blurb: The Lost Sierra covers the meeting zone of the Sierra Nevada and Cascade ranges in Northeast California, running north from Tahoe toward Lassen, with many crags in and around Plumas National Forest. It is a scattered, varied region of two dozen sub-areas. Bouldering is the biggest share, followed by sport, trad and top-rope. Sport climbing concentrates at The Mill and Grizzly Dome, while Bald Rock, in the lower foothills, pairs longer trad climbs with a good number of boulder problems. Upper Bidwell Park, the Bucks Lake zones and Oroville Boulders add more variety. Roped climbs mostly sit between 5.8 and 5.12, with boulders from V0 up to about V6.

oh_eastern_ohio.blurb: Eastern Ohio sits on the edge of Appalachia, within reach of Interstate 70, and offers almost nothing but bouldering on sandstone. Salt Fork State Park and Raven Rocks are the two main destinations, with smaller spots at Piatt Park, Coal Train Boulder and Long Run Boulders. The stone at Salt Fork is solid and well featured, noticeably less crumbly than some other Ohio sandstone, with problems from the easiest grades up to hard projects and plenty of room for further development. Across the region most problems fall between V0 and V5, with a tail reaching V10, so there is a fine spread for newer boulderers as well as strong ones.

ky_foxtown_boulders.blurb: Foxtown Boulders is a bouldering-only area in Daniel Boone National Forest, around fifteen minutes by road from McKee, Kentucky. It is still growing, with new problems and areas turning up regularly. Grades are mostly V0 to V5, with a thinner tail reaching V8. Biosphere is the largest sector and is split into six smaller ones, while Walkers Branch and Sacred Ruins add more, and The Crypt sits on a cliff above two other areas, sunny and with views over the valley. Boulders are spread over many pockets, with walks that range from seconds to half an hour.

ca_culp_valley.blurb: Culp Valley is a granite bouldering area in the desert of San Diego County, along the S-22 road above Borrego Springs near Ranchita, at about 3,000 feet. The desert setting brings views toward the Salton Sea. Nearly all of it is bouldering, with only a few top-rope, sport and trad routes. Problems run from V0 up to V10, with the largest share at the easy to moderate end, so beginners have plenty to try alongside harder lines. CVPC, Cottonwood Area, Windy Boulders and the Sandbag Deluxe Circuit are the biggest clusters. The granite is typical Southern California desert stone, and winter is the best season, before the heat sets in.
